chapterTitle: Chapter 1: The Winged Whales resting ground (Ceres)
editorText:
The airlock status indicator eased down from the active status as the internal pressure matched that of the Balaenoptera’s halls. John checked the recruits packing up on the range from the live feed in the airlock, disconnected his helmet and placed it in an automated mag lev pod that would soon return his suit to the tech service bay where it would then find its way to John’s designated jump bay location alongside his team’s. He took a deep breath, sighed, then opened the airlock.

As the airlock doors opened, a light fog bellowed out from the airlock into the Balaenoptera’s main transit hall. The cold air of the airlock clashed with the more human-friendly temperature of the hall.

Standing gracefully before him, a tall yet frail figure waited patiently. A smirk across her weathered face, the lady stepped to the side, presenting her palm to John as he stepped out of the airlock.

“Captain Walker,” Lady Ava said gently. John raised his hand to meet hers with a gentle clasp. John stepped out from the airlock, his eyes meeting hers with a brief respectful gaze, complimented with a soft smile.

“Lady Ava, what calls for concern? As much as I do enjoy our talks, we’ve been short-strawed another one of Marcellus’s secret missions early morning.”

The pair walked back down the halls of the protectant flagship to John’s quarters as they exchanged small talk in the open yet surprisingly empty halls.

“I see they still have you on regular recruit training duties,” John seemed un-phased by this remark.

“It’s a welcome change of pace from the usual peacekeeping deployments, I can tell you that much.” There was a slight annoyance in John’s tone, like he knew she was about to part some side objective on him.

“Do you know anything about the new security clearance they’ve placed on accessing the asteroid interceptors’ firing logs? We tried to check them out earlier while we were waiting for the recruits. It seems all access has been recently barred.”

“You know yourself, John, even with my political sway, the reach of my birds on this ship has always had some limits, but that’s not to say I can’t go digging.”

“Let’s wait till we are at my quarters before going into too much detail. We don’t know who could be eavesdropping.”

“Cautious as always, why has it got you so riled up?”

“I thought transparency was something that was a guarantee when you operate at our level.”

John had a hint of disappointment in his tone.

As he arrived at his door, he scanned his wrist while looking into the retinal scanner. A swift series of beeps confirmed his presence. His door swiftly opened, and he entered, then started removing items, packing down for bed. His room was pristine and organised, with few personal items to be seen other than a few photos of close family.

Ava paced over to the window in John’s cabin, looking out over the remaining cadets collecting themselves on the hull having completed the training session. She couldn’t hear the footsteps, but she could see them growing tiresome. She was too, she thought to herself. It was late, and she wanted to ease John’s mind so she could return to her cell herself. Politics of an ever-expanding front, while keeping the Protectant in check, laid heavy upon her, and John could see it vaguely when she finished talking.

“I see your concern, although, John,” said Ava. She paused for a moment, taking time to recall the past in her weary state, then continued.

“You know the designs of the turrets are not far dissimilar from those used in the previous war. Rail rifle technology—Japan always had a knack for producing the finest rail technology. The first to click onto it, actually. You ever wonder why Tau is so good at what she does?”

Lady Meera paused, awaiting John’s response.

“I always took her for the Engineer when I first met her,” said John.

“Well,” said Ava, “at this point, you might as well say the Protectant had met a plateau in their engineering prowess. Modularity, robustness—it had been engineered in as a staple of the Solar expansion. Waste was merely something of the past.”

She paced over to John’s study, where he had portraits of his family laid out on his wall.

“Aaah yes, she was a beauty—your mother, that photo. When was it taken, do you know?” Ava gleaned in closer to the portrait. She could see a young happy boy, his dad’s hand resting on his shoulder.

“Not sure,” said John. “the end of the 21st century, I think.”

“Over half a century ago. I tend to lose track of time so easily... with the resleeving process and all.”

“What sleeve number are you on now?”

“All original, believe it or not… I could never get behind the whole feeling of being in a young body again. I believe, as a political figure, despite how many parties have used it to rally against me, being old... not with the times. Hell, my mind retains my experience, the body shows it in lessons learned on the skin.”

“It’s paid off though, it seems, Lady Ava,” said John.

Ava humbly replied, “Well... I still have a few tricks up my sleeves, John Walker, don’t you worry about that...”

John was enjoying Lady Ava’s company a little more now. He felt at home in a sense with her, and he couldn’t tell exactly why for a moment.

“I knew your mother personally. She was a great woman.”

“I haven’t heard from her since the worker bot program was decommissioned.”

“Are you not at all curious as to why?”

“My mother never really had much to do with me since I left for Protectant training. Don’t think she really approved of my choices. I was 17, fresh out of college.”

“Now now, I am sure that wasn’t the case. She probably just got caught up in her work more than anything.” Ava was kind in her tone; you could tell she thought highly of John’s mother.

“She would be proud to see how far you’ve come.”

John didn’t know exactly how to feel. He was silent for a moment.

“I don’t remember much of my mother. I recall in my junior years before I turned 13, I would often be on the farm riding my race horse Beverly.”

“Oh yes, I recall. She had a thing for velocity, your mother.”

John paused for a minute. He seemed surprised.

“You... you worked with mother?”

“In my younger days, yes. We were quite the team, me and your mother, you know.”

“I didn’t realise you had a knack for technology.”

“Welll.. It wasn’t entirely technical the role, I was more in the political side of sorts”,”I See”, “Don’t worry, it didn’t stop me from having to get my hands dirty don’t you worry about that”. John layed down on his bunk, the navy blue mattress as rigid as it was, and routine in it’s aesthetic, John couldn’t help but feel it didn’t entirely feel like home, as familiar the bulkhead was to hi. Lady Ava glanced over at the seat beside the Hull window. “Actually, she made a shit storm for me your mother” Lady Meera chuckled as she paced back to the port window. “It seems like such an age ago, I can only wonder what she is up to now”, “Like I said, haven’t heard from her since I left for protectant training”, “I have a strange feeling that her works are still very present in the universe, even after her project was decommissioned”, “Project?” John pondered what on earth she could be talking about. “The Serva Vitae Project.. She had high hopes your mother, much like your father I believe, probably why they gravitated to one another. It’s no surprise really, with radical advancement, it seems there is always some radical response by the current algorithm, Technocrats couldn’t keep up if you ask me” “People are afraid of what they don’t understand” Said John “You should see the way the new recruits looked at us when we said we were jettisoning them off the ship and another person would be commandeering their suits” “Well, I can assure you John, nothing scared your mother, not even losing her job it seems”, “Sounds like her, we once had a horse break out of it’s pen, thing was rabbid, she just stood there and stared it straight in the eyes, I didn’t think she was breathing…” “Let me guess.. ” Said Ava. “The horse walked back into it’s pen”. “How did you know?”, “Oh I know the look she gave the horse, infact the look she gave your friend Marcellus” “I see.. ” Said John.

“How did he handle that?” “Funnily enough it worked… of course until the horse realised she wasn’t bluffing” “Bluffing?” “Lets just say your mother was hard to contain in her work, a wildcard. She paid dearly for it. It was the back chatter around then… I like to think she quietly slipped out the back door between me and you.. John” John turned his head to make eye contact with Ava, she let out a slight smirk, like she was up to something. But he couldn’t put his finger on it.

“Yes those were the old days we had only just broken the 3rd quarter of the 21st century. The economy struggled initially for a short while with the onset and testing of the new economy caused some minor conflicts on small fronts contained by the rapidly developing protectant and it’s rapidly expanding empire some might say. Then you had the Technocrats that justified the fluctuations had to be accounted for but the economy that tried to keep up. The Federation collectively had focused resources on Exploration, and in doing so solved several shortfalls along the way.. But lets not get carried away with economy, It seems they can’t afford to be releasing the vector data of those Asteroid interceptors to a new threat!” Ava paused for a moment. “Whatever you do down there John tomorrow, be careful.. I have a feeling that we are being watched,” “you think there’s an insider?” “Not in your immediate squad” Meera’s eyes fixed softly with johns “But I needn’t think you should worry about it”

John sat quietly for a moment, absorbing Ava’s words. The soft hum of the ship's systems played in the background, faint vibrations running through the floor like a heartbeat—steady, controlled, but ever-present.

He looked out through the other observation port, his gaze drawn to the distant asteroid fields glinting faintly against the void. The protectant, the Federation, the economy—words that used to mean something tangible now seemed like faint echoes of a world long past. Out here, in the dark, the only currency that mattered was trust, and even that felt thinly stretched.

“You think they’re tracking us already?” John asked, breaking the silence. His voice was calm, measured, but the slight crease in his brow betrayed his unease.

Lady Meera tilted her head, her expression unreadable as she leaned against the bulkhead. “Tracking? No,” she said softly. “It’s not that simple. Surveillance isn’t just about sensors or signals anymore. It’s about patterns. Behaviors. Movements. A system designed to predict, not just observe.”

John's fingers drummed lightly on the edge of the console. “You’re talking about behavioral algorithms, aren’t you?”

Ava nodded. “Exactly. They don’t need a direct line on you when they can predict where you’ll be, what you’ll do. And those asteroid interceptors... if the data leaks, it’s not just about one mission. It’s the whole defense network. Vulnerable.”

Ava, who had been silent till now, finally spoke, her voice carrying a note of sarcasm to cut through the tension. “Well, let’s hope they didn’t base the algorithms on John’s erratic behavior. Otherwise, we’re doomed.”

John smirked, but the levity didn’t last long. “Who’s the threat, then? Meera, if it’s not an insider, then what?”

Meera hesitated, her eyes drifting to the faint star trails streaking the darkness outside. “Sometimes,” she said slowly, “it’s not about who. It’s about what.”

That word hung in the air between them. What. John didn’t need her to elaborate. He knew what she meant. Artificial systems, rogue constructs, black-box entities—they weren’t enemies you could negotiate with or out think. They just were. Relentless. Logical to a fault. And completely alien in their objectives.

“You think the Federation lost control of something?” he asked finally.

Lady Ava’s silence was answer enough.

Ava looked between them, her usual sharp wit tempered now by a quiet unease. “You really know how to ruin the pre-mission vibes, don’t you?”

Ava stood, a smile drew accross her weathered cheeks as she rose, her exotic dress elegantly glid accross in her wake as she made her way to the exit expression hardening. “Whatever it is,” he said, his voice firm now, “we deal with it tomorrow. Like we always do.”

But as she walked toward the hatch, Meera’s parting words stopped his confidence for a moment. “Just remember, John,” she said softly, “even if you don’t trust the system, trust your squad. The moment you start doubting them is the moment you lose.”

John nodded closing his eyes, his jaw Loosening. Trust. It was a currency he couldn’t afford to lose—not tomorrow, not ever
